quests.persona: a coworker who takes an unusually long time to reply to messages
quests.scene: You've been waiting two days for a reply from a coworker on something you need for your own deadline tomorrow.
options: Hi again — just following up, since I need this for tomorrow's deadline. Any chance you could get back to me today?
Hey, just checking in, I suppose, I was going more on instinct than anything, though I'm open to changing my mind — and there's a decent chance I'd see it differently after sleeping on it.
I've messaged you twice now and haven't heard anything, this is honestly really frustrating.
quests.hint: When following up on something urgent, restate the deadline clearly so the other person understands why a quick reply matters.
quests.explanation: Restating the deadline clearly gives your coworker a real, specific reason to prioritize a reply today. A vague follow-up doesn't convey the actual time pressure you're under. Leading with frustration, even if justified, may make your coworker defensive rather than prompt them to help quickly.
consequencePreviews: As a result, you follow up clearly and explain the urgency, which gives your coworker a real reason to prioritize replying.
You may notice that the vague follow-up doesn't convey the actual urgency, so your coworker may not realize it's time-sensitive.
Here, leading with frustration may put your coworker on the defensive rather than prompting a quick, helpful response.

quests.persona: a professor who hasn't responded to an important email
quests.scene: You emailed a professor five days ago asking about an assignment extension, and the deadline is tomorrow.
options: Hi, just checking on my email, thinking about it now, I wasn't considering every angle, but that could easily change — and I'm honestly still working out how I feel about the whole thing.
Hi Professor Lin, following up on my email from Monday about a possible extension — the deadline is tomorrow, so I wanted to check before then if possible.
I sent an email five days ago and still haven't heard back, which is a bit frustrating given the deadline is tomorrow, to be fair, I hadn't weighed all the details.
quests.hint: When following up with someone senior about a time-sensitive request, restate the context and deadline clearly and professionally.
quests.explanation: Restating the context and the deadline clearly and professionally gives the professor everything they need to respond in time. A vague follow-up risks the professor not even remembering what the original email was about. Expressing frustration, even mildly, may come across as more confrontational than is appropriate for this relationship.
consequencePreviews: As a result, the vague follow-up doesn't remind the professor what the email was about or that it's time-sensitive.
Here, you provide the context and urgency clearly, giving the professor what they need to respond in time.
You may notice that leading with frustration toward a professor may come across as more confrontational than the situation calls for.

quests.persona: a vendor who has missed two agreed deadlines already
quests.scene: A vendor has already missed two agreed deadlines for a deliverable your team is depending on, and you're following up a third time.
options: Just checking in on this again, in hindsight, I hadn't weighed all the details, so I could be wrong — and I know that's not the most thought-out response, but it's where my head's at right now, and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.
This is honestly unacceptable, you keep missing every deadline you give us.

This is the third time we've had to follow up on this deliverable, and it's now affecting our own timeline. Could you give me a firm date today, and let me know if there's a blocker we should be aware of?
quests.hint: When a pattern of missed deadlines has real consequences, name the pattern factually, state the impact, and ask for a firm commitment and any blockers.
quests.explanation: Naming the pattern factually, stating the real impact, and asking for both a firm date and any blockers is direct without being purely accusatory, and it's more likely to get real results. A soft, generic follow-up doesn't reflect how serious the pattern has actually become. A strong accusation might feel justified, but it risks the vendor becoming defensive instead of focused on actually solving the underlying issue.
consequencePreviews: As a result, the soft follow-up doesn't reflect the seriousness of a pattern that's now genuinely affecting your own team's work.
The strong accusation may make the vendor defensive rather than motivated to actually solve the underlying problem.
As a result, you name the pattern factually, state the real impact, and ask for both a firm commitment and any underlying reason.

quests.persona: a manager assigning surprise weekend work
quests.scene: Your manager messages Friday evening: 'Could you take a look at the Renwick file over the weekend? Nothing urgent, just when you get a chance.'
options: Sure, I'll get to it, to be honest, I was just going with my gut on that one, so let me know if that's off — and there's a decent chance I'd see it differently after sleeping on it.
I can take a look Monday morning first thing — is that soon enough, or is there something time-sensitive I'm missing?
I'd rather not work on weekends if it's not urgent, I guess, I wasn't considering every angle, so I could be wrong — and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet.
quests.hint: When asked to do non-urgent work on your own time, propose a specific alternative time rather than a vague agreement or an open-ended decline.
quests.explanation: Proposing a specific time and confirming there's no hidden urgency protects your weekend while still being responsive. Agreeing vaguely risks setting an expectation of weekend work that wasn't actually necessary. Declining without offering an alternative time leaves the request only half-resolved, when a simple Monday morning slot would have worked.
consequencePreviews: As a result, agreeing vaguely may set an expectation that you'll work over the weekend, even though your manager said it wasn't urgent.
As a result, you protect your weekend while checking whether there's a real deadline you should know about.
In this moment, the statement is reasonable but doesn't offer a specific alternative time, which leaves the request somewhat unresolved.

quests.persona: a classmate asking for help outside of normal hours
quests.scene: A classmate messages you at 11pm: 'Sorry to bother you so late, could you help me understand this concept before tomorrow's quiz?'
options: No worries — I can't tonight, it's pretty late for me, but I'm free at 7am before class if that still works for you.

Sure, give me a minute, actually, I hadn't stopped to think it all the way through, so take it with a grain of salt — and I know that's not the most thought-out response, but it's where my head's at right now.
It's pretty late, I don't think I can help right now.
quests.hint: When a late-night request doesn't work for you, decline the timing specifically but offer a genuine alternative that still helps.
quests.explanation: Declining the late hour while offering a specific, genuine alternative respects your own time while still being helpful. Agreeing despite being genuinely tired isn't sustainable and could lead to resentment building over repeated late requests. Declining without any alternative leaves your classmate without help, even though a workable option — like early morning — was actually available.
consequencePreviews: As a result, you protect your own evening while offering a genuine, specific alternative that still helps before the quiz.
Agreeing despite it being very late for you may not be sustainable and could lead to resentment over time.
Realistically, the decline is reasonable but doesn't offer any alternative, even though the quiz is still tomorrow.

quests.persona: a manager who repeatedly messages you about work during evenings and weekends
quests.scene: Your manager has messaged you about non-urgent work matters during evenings and weekends several times this month. Tonight's message says: 'Just thinking about the Castellan proposal, any early thoughts?'
options: I really wish you'd stop messaging me outside work hours, it's becoming a problem.
Sure, let me think about that now.
I'll have some solid thoughts for you first thing tomorrow — I've been trying to keep evenings work-free lately so I can actually focus during the day, hope that's okay.
quests.hint: When a pattern of after-hours messages has built up, you can set a boundary gently, in the moment, without turning it into a big confrontation.
quests.explanation: Gently setting the boundary in the moment, framed around your own focus rather than a complaint, addresses the pattern without making it a confrontation. Responding to the work question anyway reinforces exactly the pattern you'd probably rather change. A direct, pointed confrontation about the pattern may feel more intense than necessary and could strain what's otherwise a normal working relationship.
consequencePreviews: Realistically, the direct confrontation, especially over a single message, may feel more intense than the situation calls for and could strain the relationship.
In this moment, continuing to respond in the evening reinforces the pattern, making it less likely to change going forward.
Realistically, you address the pattern gently and set a genuine, sustainable boundary, without making it feel like a confrontation over one message.
